questions.q: Which alkane CANNOT be prepared by the Wurtz reaction?
questions.explain: The Wurtz reaction always joins two alkyl groups, so the smallest possible product is ethane, from a methyl halide. Methane has only one carbon and cannot form this way.

questions.q: The halide shown is treated with sodium in dry ether. The product is:
questions.explain: Two isopropyl groups join through the carbons that carried chlorine: 2 (CH₃)₂CHCl + 2Na → (CH₃)₂CH–CH(CH₃)₂ + 2NaCl. The straight chain n-hexane would need 1-chloropropane.

questions.q: A mixture of bromomethane and bromoethane is treated with sodium in dry ether. The alkanes formed are:
questions.explain: Each halide can couple with itself or with the other, giving ethane (CH₃–CH₃), propane (CH₃–C₂H₅) and butane (C₂H₅–C₂H₅). This mixture is why the Wurtz reaction is not used for odd-carbon alkanes; Corey–House is the clean route.

questions.q: The dihalide shown is treated with sodium in refluxing dioxane. The main product is:
options: A bicyclobutyl with both Cl atoms kept
questions.explain: Under these conditions the intramolecular Wurtz reaction joins C-1 and C-3 of the same ring, closing bicyclo[1.1.0]butane in about 95% yield. The bicyclobutyl (coupling at C–Br of two molecules) is the exam answer for Na/ether at low temperature.
